title: Booksellers suspect AI firms are buying and then destroying rare books
gist: Rare booksellers are now treating unhaggled bulk orders as a red flag for AI training buyers — Ireland's Kennys flagged a 5,000-title order — while non-destructive alternatives from Google's 2009 patent and the Internet Archive's hand-scanning exist but lose on cost and speed to spine-cutting.

insights.claim: Cutting spines and trashing scanned pages persists because it is simply the cheapest and fastest way to digitize books at scale, and AI firms are racing to train on the long-form high-quality text only books contain.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Destruction is a cost-optimization outcome, not malice — so it only stops if the cost differential closes or reputational/legal cost rises above it.
insights.quote: But that’s the cheapest and easiest way to scan books as fast as possible, and AI companies are in a race to advance their models by training on the kind of engaging, high-quality long-form texts that can only be found in books.
insights.locator: It’s indeed depressing to imagine piles of book spines

insights.claim: Google patented a non-destructive book-scanning technology back in 2009 that AI firms could adopt, but it introduces page-curve text distortion, missed pages, and worker-speed glitches including disembodied hands obscuring pages.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The technical alternative has existed for 17 years and is not adopted — evidence that data-quality tolerance, not technical capability, drives the choice.
insights.quote: Google patented a non-destructive book-scanning technology in 2009 that AI firms could use to efficiently scan books—if they were willing to slow down and invest in the process.
insights.locator: What makes this destruction extra painful

insights.claim: The Internet Archive tested commercial book scanners with vacuum-powered page-turning arms and found automation failed on brittle books, rare volumes and special collections — the exact material libraries most want digitized.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Automation fails hardest on the highest-value corpus, meaning rare-book digitization stays labor-intensive and expensive regardless of AI budgets.
insights.quote: it turns out those automated scanners didn’t really work well for brittle books, rare volumes, and other special collections—the kinds of material our library partners ask us to digitize
insights.locator: The Internet Archive did try going the automated route

insights.claim: The Internet Archive's process is deliberately manual — foot-pedal glass lifting, per-page camera adjustment, foldout tracking, and proprietary software that halts and re-prompts on any skipped or blurry page — with one scanner, Eliza Zhang, having handled more than 3 million pages, 14,000 foldouts and 18,000 items since 2010.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Concrete throughput numbers give the benchmark against which AI-scale digitization economics can actually be compared — roughly 300,000 pages a year per skilled operator.
insights.quote: more than 3 million pages, 14,000 foldouts, and 18,000 items (mostly books)
insights.locator: At the time, Zhang had scanned

insights.claim: Rare booksellers have developed a heuristic for spotting AI buyers: genuine collectors seek single titles, while suspicious orders are large batches of widely varying selections — and crucially, the buyer makes no attempt to haggle on price.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Price-insensitivity as a detection signal means AI buyers will have to start haggling to stay hidden — a small but real friction cost being imposed on data acquisition.
insights.quote: this order seemed suspicious because the buyer made no attempt to haggle on the price—which has now become an obvious “red flag” that AI is potentially involved
insights.locator: Meanwhile, rare booksellers continue to flag strange orders

insights.claim: The Irish bookstore Kennys flagged an order for 5,000 obscure titles as "bananas," and Tomás Kenny says he plans to refuse orders likely destined for AI training to protect authors' rights and reader access.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sellers unilaterally refusing sales is a supply-channel closure that no licensing deal or copyright ruling addresses — a physical bottleneck on the scanned-book corpus.
insights.quote: if they are taking a book and scanning it with a view to taking intellectual property, then Kennys do not want to be a part of that
insights.locator: Tomás Kenny of Kennys Bookshop told the Times

insights.claim: Booksellers face an explicit short-term-gain versus long-term-survival tradeoff: large orders help revenue now, but selling into indiscriminate destruction may mean they are signing their own death warrant.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: When suppliers believe a customer is destroying their own future inventory, they exit the trade — the same dynamic that ends any extractive procurement relationship.
insights.quote: may be signing their own death warrant
insights.locator: Although some booksellers said they could benefit

insights.claim: The intermediation layer is also under scrutiny: 404 Media reported that book-database company ISBNdb was advertising that it could help AI firms source books in bulk, and ISBNdb reportedly warned clients the optics were bad.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Data brokers sitting between AI buyers and physical supply are the choke point where either regulation or reputational pressure will bite first.
insights.quote: then 404 Media reported that a book-database company called ISBNdb was advertising that it could help AI firms source books in bulk
insights.locator: As The Atlantic reported last week

insights.claim: A summer 2025 lawsuit outed Anthropic for destroying millions of print books to train its models, and the company used the internal codename "Project Panama" for its destructive scanning specifically to keep the practice hidden from the public.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Codenaming a legal-but-unpopular practice is evidence firms internally price the reputational risk — a predictor of where the next disclosure fight lands.
insights.quote: Anthropic started using a codename—“Project Panama”—for its destructive book-scanning in an effort to keep it hidden from the public.

insights.claim: The article explicitly notes there is no indication Anthropic ever destroyed rare books and that the company has denied doing so — a distinction between destroying ordinary purchased copies and destroying irreplaceable ones.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The rare-versus-common distinction is where the real dispute sits; conflating them overstates the harm and muddies which practices actually warrant intervention.
insights.quote: There is no indication that Anthropic ever destroyed rare books, and the company has denied doing so in statements.
insights.locator: There is no indication that Anthropic ever destroyed rare books

insights.claim: Elon Musk publicly stated he asked his team to preserve rare books in a library and scan them the hard way rather than cutting off spines, but critics note he never said xAI would not destroy any books and never defined "rare."
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Undefined preservation pledges are unenforceable and unmeasurable — treat them as PR until a firm publishes a definition and an audit trail.
insights.quote: asked the SpaceXAI team to preserve any rare books in a library and scan them the hard way vs just cutting off the spine and scanning

insights.claim: Copyright law permits AI firms to destroy copies of books they have purchased, so the constraint on this practice is public pressure and supplier refusal rather than legal prohibition.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: With the legal path closed, the entire fight moves to procurement and reputation — which is why bookseller behavior is the variable that actually matters.
insights.quote: even if copyright law allows them to destroy copies of books they’ve purchased
insights.locator: But not everyone is convinced that the biggest AI firms are sincere

insights.claim: OpenAI and Microsoft are working with Harvard librarians to train models on roughly 1 million public-domain books dating back to the 15th century — a preservation-compatible sourcing path distinct from bulk purchase and destruction.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Institutional public-domain partnerships are the sanctioned model likely to become the industry standard once reputational costs bite; watch for more library-lab deals.
insights.quote: OpenAI and Microsoft, for example, are working with Harvard librarians on an initiative to train AI models on about 1 million public-domain books dating back to the 15th century.
insights.locator: It’s also true that some AI firms are helping preserve rare books.

insights.claim: The Internet Archive's core operating principle is that careful handling requires human judgment — clean, dry human hands are its stated best method for turning pages, a constraint that structurally caps throughput.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: If preservation-grade digitization cannot be automated, then any policy requiring it functions as a hard rate limit on AI book corpora.
insights.quote: clean, dry human hands are the best way to turn pages

insights.claim: The author's stated hope is that public backlash pressures the largest AI firms into adopting Internet Archive-style methods that preserve books physically as well as digitally.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Backlash-driven method change is the optimistic scenario; the base case remains cost-driven destruction until a supplier or regulator forces the issue.
insights.quote: It’s possible that public backlash will pressure the biggest firms to adopt methods like the Internet Archive’s, which focus as much on preserving rare books physically as they do digitally.
insights.locator: It’s possible that public backlash will pressure the biggest firms
